text: The Wall comes down and one woman in Berlin takes it as a bereavement. Flanders is a novelist whose name the public knows; she believed in the East German state, and she reaches the capital in time to watch that belief dissolve into everyone else's celebration. Oskar Roehler builds the film from encounters — acquaintances, strangers, the return trip to Munich — and each runs aground on the same difficulty: her grief has no audience in 1989. The result sits closer to comedy than to elegy, which is the more uncomfortable choice. The German Film Award it took for best feature is a strange laurel for a portrait this unaccommodating. What stays is a woman explaining herself to rooms that have already moved on, and doing it in complete sentences.

A woman takes the six-month-old daughter of the man she has been having an affair with, and raises her as her own. What follows is not a manhunt. Izuru Narushima spends 147 minutes on what the theft buys — four years of feeding and hiding and moving, a household of two living under invented names, and a child for whom the kidnapper is simply the person who is there. The crime supplies a clock; the drama is everything the clock measures. What the film asks is difficult: that the arrangement be allowed to look domestic, even well run, even happy, while the fact underneath it never changes shape. Tenderness and theft are made of the same material here, and neither is offered as an excuse for the other.

A trekking guide flies to Bangkok to repair a love affair, and the woman who asked for the meeting never arrives. What takes her place is a mistaken identity that will not be corrected: strangers greet Shakthi as a millionaire businessman and go on greeting him that way, until the guide starts to look like the weaker of the two claims. Thiru keeps the tourist surfaces — hotels, a city the hero has no history in, a new acquaintance called Maya — and lets them thin out into a place where nothing confirms anything. Then the genre machinery arrives, as it must in a Tamil action thriller of this length, and the chases take their turn. The question underneath survives them: what a man can produce as evidence of himself, once everyone around him has decided otherwise.

A bullock cart travels at the speed of the bullock, and a film that seats its lovers in one has agreed to that speed. The driver is a countryman with no talent for concealment. His passenger is a dancer who works the fairs and moves on when they close, and Basu Bhattacharya keeps them on the road between engagements, talking, because on a cart there is nothing else to do. The distance between them is not age or class so much as practice: she has learned what to show, and he has not. That is where the comedy lives. It is also where the injury is. Two and a half hours of road, and the patience is not decorative — it is the only way a romance built from small courtesies and long silences becomes legible at all.

The visa is good for three months, and the second half of the film is about what those three months bought. Fruit Chan cuts the picture in two. First Hong Kong: rented rooms, back alleys, a young woman from the northern mainland working against a clock in a trade the city depends on and prefers not to name. Then the Northeast, where she goes home to family and an ex-fiancé and winter streets, carrying money that now has to be turned into something with a future. The second half is the stranger one, and it declines both confession and punishment: what she did is treated as work that ended, and the film follows what a person builds with the proceeds. The border between the halves is administrative, not moral — which is how it works for the people crossing it.

A reporter named Erika starts pulling at a government cover-up, and the man on the other side of it has a name, Sugihara, and a chain of command. Michihito Fujii gives the bureaucrat close to the attention he gives the journalist, which is what keeps the film out of newsroom heroics: one of them is trying to get a story into print, the other is doing what his office requires, and the collision is a matter of institutions rather than villainy. Neither is written as a monster. The texture is deliberately unglamorous — desks, corridors, the slow business of confirming a thing twice — and the anxiety in it is procedural. The Japan Academy named it picture of the year, an odd fate for a film whose argument is that official silence is not a scandal but a working method.

From the Japanese invasion through the surrender of 1945 and into what came after: ninety-four minutes for all of it. Yim Ho keeps most of the war offscreen and puts a novelist and a man working for the occupation in rooms together, which is the more dangerous address in any case. History reaches them as a change in what can be said aloud, then as a change in who is permitted to say it. She writes; he collaborates; the affair is never granted the privacy it wants. The compression shows, and the film uses it — scenes stop early, years fall between cuts, and the two keep having to meet again as slightly altered people. A romance is a poor instrument for measuring two decades of a country's history, and this one is honest about the poor fit, and proceeds anyway.

A silk weaver makes cloth he will never own, and promises his newborn daughter that she will be married in it. That promise is the engine: a girl's childhood becomes the term of a debt, and Priyadarshan counts the years in what a loom pays against what a household costs. Everything around the man is arranged to make the promise impossible — the wage, the buyer, the whole structure that hands the finished silk to somebody else. Kanchivaram is unhurried about that arithmetic, which is right, since the pressure comes from ordinary weeks and not from crises. Nor is the weaver ennobled by his own vow. A promise of that size, carried across an entire childhood, narrows the man carrying it, and the film is willing to watch the narrowing happen.

Nagisa grew up in Hiroshima as a son and now lives in Shinjuku as a woman. That is where the film begins rather than what it is about; what it wants is the accident that lands a neglected middle-school girl, a distant relative, in her rooms. Ichika's mother has stopped looking after her. Nagisa has never looked after anyone. Eiji Uchida lets the arrangement stay awkward for a long stretch — two people who did not choose each other, working out a routine without any vocabulary for what they are to one another — and the turn, when it comes, arrives slowly and without announcement. Tokyo here is rented rooms, trains and school hours. The film treats a woman's late and inconvenient arrival at motherhood as an event with consequences, not as a lesson to be drawn.

The backwaters of Kerala are a working road, and the man in this film earns his living moving along them. Kutty Srank is short-tempered, solitary and careful to stay on the right side of the law, which is a difficult set of traits to sit beside for two hours unless the film is patient. Shaji N. Karun is patient. The premise commits him to a route instead of a plot: water, cargo, the landings where a boat ties up, and people who get a stretch of this man's company and then watch him go. Landscape here is labour — the current, the hours, the weather that decides whether a day is possible. Across 127 minutes the accumulation does the work an incident would do elsewhere, and the word lonely stops being an adjective.

Germany, 1950, and here is a family comedy whose premise is a divorce. Two nine-year-olds meet at a summer camp, one rude and one shy and otherwise the same face, and work out that they are twins: one raised by the mother, one by the father, neither ever told the other existed. Their remedy is to trade places. Josef von Báky plays the exchange for delight, and the delight is procedural — two girls teaching each other an entire life, hair and manners and the names of people they have never met, then walking into homes that will not be warned. Underneath is the thing nobody in the film says plainly, which is that two adults divided their children between them and kept quiet about it for nine years. The tone stays light. The premise never softens.

Three of the students in this school became movie stars; the film is about the man who taught them. Master Yu's Peking Opera academy is where Jackie Chan, Samo Hung and Yuen Biao trained, and Alex Law Kai-Yui, filming in 1988, keeps his attention on the teacher rather than the careers — the daily discipline, the room in which his authority was total, the business of turning students into performers. That choice is what lifts it above backstage anecdote. The famous names work mainly as evidence that the school worked; the film is far more curious about the cost of running such a place, and about what a master amounts to once the students have gone. It took best feature at the Golden Horse Awards, which is a fair reward for looking away from the marquee.

A proud old widower who has organised his life around discipline decides to take a holiday. Mrinal Sen then arranges for him to have nothing to be strict about: nobody to correct, no rules that anyone out there recognises, only open country and people entirely unimpressed by him. Ninety-six minutes, and the brevity is the method — the joke depends on a man being separated from his structure faster than he can rebuild it. The comedy is dry and a little merciless. Sen does not despise him, though, and that is the film's real risk: it lets an unenchanted man be surprised, then treats the surprise as an event rather than a punchline, which requires believing that a rigid person can be caught off guard without being humiliated.

The mother is a famous dancer; the daughter is the one who was at home while the career was being built. Rituparno Ghosh puts them in the same flat and lets an old complaint surface in ordinary registers — timing, politeness, the particular rudeness available to a grown child. There is almost no exterior and almost no incident. A Bengali chamber piece from 1993, it rests on two performances and the furniture, which is a demanding way to fill a film. What saves it from being a prosecution is that the dancing counts as work: the fame was earned, and it was earned with hours the daughter spent by herself, and the film declines to rule on which of those facts outranks the other. Neither woman is given the comfort of being simply wronged.
